title: Test a lead-acid battery
summary: Find out whether a salvaged lead-acid battery is worth carrying: inspect it, read its resting voltage, check each cell with a hydrometer if it has caps, charge it, then see whether it holds up under load and keeps its charge for a few days.

materials.item: 12 V load such as a car headlight bulb (about 55–60 W) with two wires and clips
Battery hydrometer, for batteries with removable caps
Baking soda and clean water for spills

steps.text: Put on glasses and gloves. Inspect: cracks, bulges, leaks, melted or loose terminals, a warped case. Reject cracked or bulging batteries.
steps.warn: The outside of an old battery may be coated in acid.

steps.text: Look for a date code or sticker. Batteries more than about 5 years old are often near the end even if they read well.
Measure the resting voltage on DC volts. If the battery has sat for hours, compare it with the table in the notes to judge its charge.
On flooded batteries with caps, check the acid covers the plates. Test each cell with the hydrometer. All cells should read within about 0.05 of each other. One low cell means a bad cell.
steps.warn: Acid drips from the hydrometer. Hold it over the battery and squeeze the bulb slowly.

steps.text: Charge it fully with a proper charger in a ventilated place. A battery that gets hot, or bubbles hard in one cell only, is failing.
steps.warn: Charging makes hydrogen: no sparks or flames. Never charge a frozen battery.

steps.text: Let it rest at least 12 hours after charging, then measure. A good 12 V battery reads 12.6 V or more (AGM types a little higher). Below about 10.5 V after charging usually means a shorted cell.

Load test: connect the headlight bulb and watch the voltage. A healthy, fully charged battery stays above about 12 V for the first 15 minutes. If it falls below about 11.5 V within a few minutes, it has little capacity left.
steps.warn: Bulbs get very hot. Lay it on metal or stone, away from the battery top.

steps.text: For a car starting battery, a real engine start is a good test: the voltage at the battery should stay above about 9.6–10 V while cranking.
Hold test: leave it disconnected for 3–7 days and measure again. A good battery stays above about 12.5 V. One that falls fast has internal leakage.
Write the date, resting voltage and load result on the battery with a marker. Store keepers charged.

notes:
## Resting voltage (12 V battery, about 25 °C, rested several hours)

| Voltage | Rough charge |
|---|---|
| 12.6 V or more | 100% |
| 12.4 V | about 75% |
| 12.2 V | about 50% |
| 12.0 V | about 25% |
| 11.9 V or less | flat |

For a 6 V battery, halve these. For 24 V, double them. Each cell is about 2.1 V when full. Different sources and battery types vary a little.

## Hydrometer readings (flooded batteries)

| Specific gravity | Rough charge |
|---|---|
| 1.265 | 100% |
| 1.225 | 75% |
| 1.190 | 50% |
| 1.155 | 25% |
| 1.120 | flat |

Some batteries use slightly stronger acid and read higher when full. The difference between cells matters more than the exact number.

## Surface charge

Right after charging or driving, a battery reads higher than its true charge. Let it rest 12 hours, or switch on headlights for a minute or two, then rest it a few minutes before measuring.

## What kills lead-acid batteries

- Sitting flat. Hard sulphate crystals form on the plates within weeks to months. A battery left flat for months rarely recovers fully.
- Freezing when flat. The case cracks and the plates buckle.
- Overcharging. It boils off water and wears the plates.
- Age and deep cycling. Starting batteries wear out fast if run flat repeatedly.

## Common mistakes

- Testing right after charging.
- Judging by voltage alone: a worn battery can show 12.6 V with no load and collapse under load.
- Putting a weak battery in a bank with good ones. It drags the whole bank down.
